title: Naming: suffixes and prefixes
note: One group per name gets the suffix: the highest on the list acid, anhydride, ester, acyl halide, amide, nitrile, aldehyde, ketone, alcohol, amine. Every other group becomes a prefix (hydroxy-, oxo-, amino-). Halogens, ethers and the C=C or C≡C are never the suffix group over these.

read.title: Who gets the suffix?
text: An IUPAC name has one suffix, so when a molecule contains several groups you must pick a winner. The ranking runs from highest to lowest: carboxylic acid, anhydride, ester, acyl halide, amide, nitrile, aldehyde, ketone, alcohol, amine. Whatever ranks highest becomes the suffix and sets the numbering; everything else is named as a prefix.

Take a chain with both a ketone and an alcohol. The ketone outranks the alcohol, so the name ends in -one, and the OH appears as hydroxy-. Likewise a molecule with an amine and an acid ends in -oic acid, with amino- as a prefix. A C=O that must be a prefix is called oxo-.

Halogens never win. Chloro- and bromo- always sit in the front of the name, and so do alkoxy- groups from ethers. Double and triple bonds are different: they change the -ane ending of the parent to -ene or -yne, but a higher group still takes the suffix and numbers the chain.
When the group is attached to a ring instead of ending a chain, the carbon of the group is not counted in the ring, so the endings become -carbaldehyde, -carboxylic acid and -carbonitrile.
